name: USGS on AI in Earth Science: Strategy, Podcasts and Machine Learning Research
title: USGS on AI in Earth Science: Strategy, Podcasts and Machine Learning Research
answer: The U.S. Geological Survey publishes an AI strategy, a two-part Eyes on Earth podcast on AI at its EROS data centre, and machine learning research papers. The most useful item for a mining reader is the geothermal favouritability study, which found that simple non-linear algorithms matched or beat complex neural networks because the input features, not the models, limited accuracy.

sections.body: These pages belong to the U.S. Geological Survey, a United States federal science bureau. They comprise a published Artificial intelligence strategy for the U.S. Geological Survey, two episodes of the Eyes on Earth podcast recorded at the USGS Earth Resources Observation and Science Center, an overview of artificial intelligence from the Center of Excellence for Geospatial Information Science, and publication records for machine learning research papers. The pages were read in October 2026. No single publication date is given for the strategy itself.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The AI strategy states that USGS staff have adopted AI in workflows for many years but that a comprehensive bureau strategy had not previously been developed. It sets five steps: build an AI workforce, adapt organisational approaches to include AI governance and communication, ensure responsible and trustworthy use, modernise computing and data infrastructure, and accelerate adoption and innovation. The podcast episodes describe AI as quickly becoming a necessary part of geospatial work at EROS. AI enabled the National Land Cover Database to become an annual product, and a second episode covers using AI to monitor Landsat satellite health, including thousands of measurements of subcomponents, and to support collision avoidance by training algorithms on debris and orbital data. CEGIS explains machine learning and ontologies and says it uses machine learning to map terrain features and analyse landscapes. A research paper on geothermal favouritability mapping in the western United States compares nine maps built with expert methods, logistic regression, XGBoost, support-vector machines and an artificial neural network.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The geothermal study reports F1 scores below 0.10 for all approaches, no improvement with increasing model complexity, and concludes that simple non-linear algorithms such as XGBoost perform equally well or better than artificial neural networks until improved feature data are available. It uses data from the USGS 2008 geothermal resource assessment and notes the training data have no negative examples and severe class imbalance. The podcast states the term AI was coined in 1956 and that Landsat satellites fly at a consistent 705-kilometer altitude. The strategy lists five steps for AI adoption.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in mining would use these pages for two things. The geothermal favouritability study is a direct analogue for mineral prospectivity modelling, and its finding that data quality, not model complexity, limits performance is a caution for anyone buying sophisticated algorithms for exploration targeting. The strategy and podcast show how a major public earth science body is governing AI adoption, modernising data infrastructure and applying machine learning to satellite and geospatial data, which is the same data layer exploration models draw on.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Mining

sections.body: The pages say nothing about mining, minerals or exploration directly. The geothermal study concerns geothermal energy, not mineral deposits, and its favouritability maps cover the western United States only. The strategy is a policy document without implementation results or dates. The podcast episodes are promotional summaries of conversations rather than technical papers, and several pages are publication records or programme overviews that link elsewhere for detail.
